title: Los Angeles: After the Water Ran Out
body:
# Los Angeles: After the Water Ran Out

Los Angeles did not flood. Los Angeles burned, dried, and then emptied at a pace that, from the inside, felt indistinguishable from normal — just another bad fire season, just another water restriction, just another year of leaving — until one day it was not normal, it was permanent, and the people who were going to leave had mostly left, and the people who remained were the people who were always going to remain regardless.

## The Water Accounting

The Colorado River Compact of 1922 allocated water that did not exist in the volume the compact assumed. This was known before the ink dried. It was known more precisely with each passing decade. The allocation persisted because the states that depended on it had political power proportional to how much they needed the fiction to remain intact.

The fiction became unsustainable in the 2080s. The Colorado River's flow, already reduced by thirty years of accelerating drought, fell to 41% of its Compact-era average. Lake Mead and Lake Powell — the reservoirs that had been California and Nevada's margin of safety — reached dead pool in 2091 and 2093 respectively. Dead pool is the point at which the water surface drops below the intake pipes: the reservoirs are still technically present, but none of their water can be extracted by the infrastructure built to extract it.

Southern California's municipalities had been implementing tiered conservation since the 2070s. By 2095, the conservation tiers had effectively become rationing. The daily per-person water allocation in Los Angeles fell to 42 liters — drinking, cooking, sanitation — in the summer of 2097. A Tier 1 GLMZ resident in the Gray Zone, managing on gray-market water access, uses approximately 50 liters per day. The comparison is not lost on historians.

The agriculture of the Central Valley — the food system that fed a continent — was the first to go, because agriculture is the largest consumer of water and the lowest-value economic use of it. Farms became unirrigable. The crops that defined the valley for a century stopped growing there. Food prices across the former United States rose approximately 340% between 2085 and 2110 as the Central Valley's contribution to the continental food supply was not replaced but simply absent.

## The Fire

The Santa Ana winds did not change. What changed was the fuel: the vegetation of coastal California, under sustained drought, became progressively drier, and progressively more continuous, and progressively less separated from the urban-wildland interface by the managed firebreaks that had previously made fire a survivable feature of the Southern California landscape.

The fires that burned through Los Angeles County in the fire seasons of 2099, 2103, 2107, and 2112 are the ones that appear in the histories. They are not the worst by acreage — several subsequent fire seasons exceeded them — but they are the ones that consumed neighborhoods that the public had believed, up to the moment they burned, to be safe. After 2107, the concept of safety as defined by proximity to a firebreak ceased to be operative in most of Southern California. Everything was the interface now.

The insurance industry's exit from the California market was formalized in 2109 when the last major insurer declined to renew residential policies in Los Angeles, Orange, and San Bernardino Counties. The announcement was made on a Friday afternoon in a regulatory filing. It received approximately six hours of media attention before the next fire started.

## The Emptying

The population of greater Los Angeles in 2080 was approximately 13 million. The population of the Los Angeles Basin communities in 2200 is estimated at 380,000 to 420,000, concentrated in the coastal communities where marine layer moisture moderates the fire risk and the desalination infrastructure maintains minimum water supply, and in the inland communities at higher elevations where water table access remains viable.

The emptying was not a migration. It was not organized. It was the aggregate of 12 million individual decisions, each one made for reasons that were immediate and personal rather than strategic: a job offer in the GLMZ, a family already relocated, a house that could not be insured and therefore could not be sold, a neighborhood that had burned and been rebuilt and burned again and was not being rebuilt this time. Each decision was rational. The sum of the decisions was a city that became, over thirty years, one-tenth of what it had been.

The people who remained have a specific relationship to the city that the people who left do not. They are not deluded about what Los Angeles is. They know it is not what it was. They stayed anyway, for reasons that are their own: because the ocean is there, and the ocean has not changed; because the mountains are there, and the dry air of late November still smells the same as it always did; because this is where they are from and where they intend to die; because leaving is a thing that other people do.

## What Los Angeles Is Now

Los Angeles retains the physical infrastructure of its former scale without the population to justify it. The freeway system — 900 kilometers of elevated and surface roadway — still exists, still connects the communities of the Basin, still carries traffic in the sense that any road with occasional use carries traffic. The Hollywood sign is still on the hill. The hill has burned twice since 2100; both times the sign was pre-removed and reinstalled. This decision — to reinstall it, twice, in a city with 400,000 people and no entertainment industry to speak of — is the kind of decision that tells you something about the people who remained.

The former studio lots of Hollywood proper are the most visited destination in present-day Los Angeles. They are ruins in the way that Roman ruins are ruins: structurally intact enough to walk through, stripped of the activity that gave them meaning, preserved in the particular amber of having been built too solidly to disappear. Sound stages stand open to the sky where the roof panels have been salvaged. The backlot permanent sets — New York streetscapes, Midwestern main streets, European village facades — are inhabited by the fauna of a landscape that has reverted to chaparral around them. Wild turkeys in a permanent fictional New York street. Coyotes under a fake Parisian café awning. The entertainment industry built these places to look real. The real world has moved in.

The Waxwing Neuromedia archive — acquired from the former studio system's successor entities in 2158 — contains every film produced in Hollywood between the late nineteenth century and the studio system's final collapse. The archive is in Chicago. The buildings that produced it are in Los Angeles, full of coyotes and turkeys, standing up because no one has found it worth the effort to take them down.
